lawyer:
M Amirul Islam with Dr Shirin Chowdhury, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
Fida M Kamal Additional Attorney-General with Syeda Afsar Jahan, Assistant Attorney-General—For Respondent No. 1
parties:
Shuddhananda Mahathero ------ Petitioner 
Vs 
Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
8. In his Affidavit-in-reply the petitioner has reiterated that the enquiry committee had no legal basis to hold enquiry into the allegations against the Executive Committee of the Sangha since the enquiry committee was formed in an inter-ministerial meeting held on 28-1-2001 under the Chairmanship of the State Minister for Religious Affairs who has no authority to form any enquiry committee. It is further stated that the petitioner's Sangha is registered under the 1961 Ordinance and under the said Ordinance it is the Registration Authority who is the Regulatory Authority and empowered to exercise all powers under the Ordinance including the power of dissolution or suspension of the Executive Committee of the registered agency as well as the power to make enquiry. It has been categorically stated in the Affidavit-in-reply that the law contemplates the holding of enquiry by the Registration Authority and suspension of the governing body on the basis of satisfaction of the said authority as to the findings of such enquiry conducted by it and in the instant case the formation of enquiry committee being without any lawful basis, any enquiry conducted by the said committee is coram non judice and therefore, the impugned order purporting to temporarily suspend the Executive Committee of the petitioner's Sangha is illegal, unlawful, malafide and beyond the purview of law. It has been further stated that since the enquiry committee was not constituted within the purview of law as contemplated under section 9(1) of the 1961 Ordinance, the Constitution of the 3-member caretaker body is also without any lawful basis. It has been stated that religious rituals and practices undertaken by the Buddhist community cannot be done by the caretaker body resulting in an interference and unwarranted obstruction in exercise of their right to profess, practice and propagate their own religion and manage their own religious institutions . 

 10. On the ground of maintainability Mr M Amirul Islam assisted by Dr Shirin Chowdhury appearing on behalf of the petitioner firstly, submits that the instant Writ Petition has been made under Article 102(1) and Article 102(2) of the Constitution. As per provisions of Article 102(1), since the fundamental right of the petitioner to practice religion as well as the right to establish, maintain and manage the religious institutions as guaranteed under Article 41 of the Constitution have been infringed by the impugned Memo therefore, it is not necessary to exhaust any alternative remedy including the alternative forum of appeal as provided under section 9(4) of the 1961 Ordinance. Secondly, the learned Advocate further submits that the instant Writ petition has also been made under Article 102(2) of the Constitution under which the High Court Division if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law may declare any act done by a person engaged in the affairs of the Republic to be unlawful and without any legal effect and in the present case the provision of appeal as stated in section 9(4) of the 1961 Ordinance not being a speedy and efficacious remedy the petitioner was constrained to come to this Court and obtain the present Rule, and in this connection he has relied upon the decisions reported in 49 DLR 400, 49 DLR 498, 19 DLR 489, 20 DLR 300 and 4 MLR (AD) 18. 

 11. Mr Amirul Islam next submits that the conditions contained in section 9 of the 1961 Ordinance not having arisen in the case of the petitioner's Sangha, the impugned Memo/ order has been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect in that there has been no irregularity of fund or maladministration in the conduct of the affairs of the Association or failure to comply with any of the provisions of law and Rules or the Ordinance itself. The learned Advocate further submits that the impugned order is illegal, malafide, vague, arbitrary and in gross violation of the principles of natural justice as no show cause notice was given to the petitioner or any chance to represent his case and that the impugned order was manipulated at the behest of interested quarters for the intention of grabbing the Sangha and, as such, liable to be set aside. The learned Advocate further submits that provisions of section 9(1) of the 1961 Ordinance as to dissolution or suspension of the Executive Committee of the Sangha vests with the Registration Authority and it is the Registration Authority who has the power to make and hold enquiry and on being satisfied from such enquiry has the power to suspend the Executive Committee of the Sangha. In the instant case, the enquiry not having been done by the Registration Authority and the enquiry conducted by another committee is coram non judice and the impugned order purporting temporarily to suspend the Executive Committee of the petitioner's Sangha on the basis of the findings of the said enquiry committee is illegal and not sustainable in law. 

 12. As against this, the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that section 9(1) of the 1961 Ordinance gives wide discretion to the Registration Authority to make enquiry as it thinks fit and on being satisfied from such enquiry that irregularities in respect of funds of the petitioner organisation had taken place or that there is maladministration in the conduct of its affairs or if certain organisation has failed to comply with the provisions of 1961 Ordinance or Rules made thereunder, it may suspend its governing body and that in the instant case the Registration Authority issued the impugned order pursuant to being satisfied that such suspension was required due to the presence of the circumstances stated in section 9(1) of the 1961 Ordinance and, as such, submits that the impugned order was rightly issued and calls for no interference by this Court. 

 18. The Registration Authority has been defined in section 2 of the 1961 Ordinance as the person authorised by the Government by notification in the official Gazette and in the present case it is the Director-General of the Ministry of Social Welfare. As per provisions of section 9(1) of the 1961 Ordinance, the Registration Authority, after making such enquiries as it may think fit, is satisfied that the conditions stated in section 7(1) of the 1961 Ordinance have not been complied with by a particular organisation, may suspend the governing body of the said organisation. It has been argued by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the enquiry must be conducted by the Registration Authority itself and form an opinion as to non-compliance of the conditions as stated in section 7(1) of the 1961 Ordinance. The learned Additional Attorney-General, on the other hand, submits that the Registration Authority has enquired into the matter himself but his satisfaction as to existence of such condition is a prerequisite before which he can suspend the governing body. According to him, the enquiries may be conducted by any authority or person as the Registration Authority thinks fit. In the instant case the enquiry committee was appointed by an inter-ministerial meeting and the committee comprised of Government officers including three members of the office of the Registration Authority. The enquiry report shows that the enquiry committee was headed by the Director of Administration and Finance of the Social Welfare Directorate with representatives from the Ministry of Religious Affairs and the Ministry of Social Welfare and a Deputy Director of the District Social Welfare Office, Dhaka and an observer from the Buddhist Kallayan Trust. The committee appears to have made detailed investigation into the affairs of the petitioner's organisation. The enquiry committee after investigation and enquiry has given charge-wise detailed report on the affairs of the organisation. It also appears from the enquiry report that the petitioner and the members of the Executive Committee were asked to comment on certain matters on which the enquiry was made and, as such, they were given adequate opportunity to give their version as to the matters enquired. The instant enquiry committee was made pursuant to various allegations and complaints against the petitioner and his Sangha, received by the Registration Authority as well as the Ministry of Religious Affairs and on receipt of such complaints and allegations the respondents had a duty to make enquiries into the allegations which appears to have been done. In the enquiry report it has been stated that one Japanese orgnisation by the name 'Rishi-kushikai' gave donation of 15,81,89,893 Yen as confirmed by the Japanese Embassy to the Sangha but during the enquiry no mention of this fund was made in the books of account of the Sangha, When the petitioner was asked verbally on this matter he was unable to give any satisfactory response. The Registration Authority after perusal of the enquiry report, found major discrepancies and formed an opinion that there has been maladministration in the conduct of the affairs of the Sangha and certain irregularities in respect of fund of the Association as well as there has been noncompliance of the provisions of section 9 of the 1961 Ordinance, as reflected in the impugned order and, as such, decided to suspend the petitioner's organisation. The Registration Authority must form an opinion that it is satisfied that the aforesaid conditions are prevailing in order to suspend the governing body, the conditions that appear to have been met in the present case. Section 9(1) of the 1961 Ordinance gives wide discretion upon the Registration Authority as to the kind of enquiry that is to be conducted and we cannot agree with the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that in every case the Registration Authority itself must conduct the enquiry which would make it impracticable and not always workable. What is essential is that the enquiry must take place and that the Registration Authority from the enquiry must be satisfied that conditions stated in section 9(1) of the 1961 Ordinance exists. In the instant case, the officers immediately subordinate to the Registration Authority were part of the enquiry team and it cannot be said that the Registration Authority was not represented in the enquiry. It is not the case of the petitioner that the enquiry itself was vitiated for being done dishonestly or malafide and, as such, the Registration Authority ought not to have relied upon the said report of the enquiry committee . Thus, we feel that the requirement of section 9(1) of the 1961 Ordinance in respect of conduct of the enquiry has been complied with and that the Registration Authority acted within its power to suspend the governing body. 

 21. In the instant case, the petitioner has alleged that his fundamental rights of practicing or propagating and professing his religion as guaranteed by Article 41 of the Constitution has been infringed by the impugned order and, as such, he has filed this Writ petition. 

 23. It appears that the petitioner's Sangha has been registered under the 1961 Ordinance as Voluntary Social Welfare Organisation. The said Ordinance specifically provides that the organisation is required to maintain audited accounts as well as to comply with other conditions as stated in section 9 of the 1961 Ordinance itself failing which the authority may suspend the governing body of the organisation and in the instant case by the impugned order the Registration Authority has done just that. The petitioner's Sangha having voluntarily chosen to register itself under the Ordinance and agreeing to comply with the terms, conditions and stipulations of the said Ordinance, once the authority exercises its powers conferred by the said Ordinance it does not lie in the mouth of the petitioner to turn back and say that the exercise of such power is an infringement of his fundamental rights as provided by the Constitution a fortiori since the petitioner's organisation is registered under the Ordinance and is not a religious organisation or formed exclusively for a small section of the community but for the whole Buddhist community. Furthermore, the petitioner has not been able to satisfy us as to how religious practice and right of the petitioner will be infringed if the caretaker body takes over the management of the Association with a view to hold election and transferring the administration and management of the organisation to a new elected body. Thus, in our view, the applicability of Article 102(1) of the Constitution is misconceived since the case of infringement of any fundamental rights as stated under Article 41 of the Constitution has not been made out. 

 24. The petitioner has also claimed to have preferred the instant application under Article 102(2) of the Constitution which empowers the High Court Division to interfere with orders of the Government functionaries when no other equally efficacious and speedy remedy is available to the petitioner and has cited the case of Acqua Food Limited and another vs Controller of Imports and Exports and others reported 49 DLR 498. In the said case it has been held that despite the availability of an alternative efficacious remedy, an application under Article 102 of the Constitution is maintainable when an administrative order is passed under the direction of a superior authority and the concerned Government functionary does not exercise his independent jurisdiction. In the instant case however, the Registration Authority has been satisfied that the conditions stated in section 7(1) of the 1961 Ordinance exists with regard to the petitioner's allegations even though the enquiry was made by a committee appointed in an inter-ministerial meeting. Therefore, we feel that the cited decision is not attracted in the instant case. 

 25. In the case of Wahidullah Majumder vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 49 DLR 400 it has been held that the availability of an alternative remedy by way of appeal or revision will not stand in the way of invoking the writ jurisdiction raising purely a question of law or interpretation of a statute. In the instant case we cannot agree with the learned Advocate for the petitioner that "interpretation of statutory provisions", particularly section 9, is involved. The language of section 9 is quite clear giving a discretion upon the Registering Authority to decide what sort of enquiry is to be made and provided he is satisfied that there has been a compliance with the conditions stated in the said section, he can suspend the governing body of the organisation which he has done in the instant case. 

 26. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has also relied upon the decision in the case of Tafijul Huq Sarker vs Bangladesh and others reported in 4 MLR (AD) 19 wherein it has been stated that when the alternative remedy is saddled with an inflexible precondition it would not be considered adequate or efficacious and, as such, an application under Article 102 of the Constitution is maintainable. For example, for preferring an appeal, if there is a non relaxable precondition of relinquishing one's office then the alternative remedy of appeal would be inadequate and not efficacious. In the instant case we do not find any inflexible precondition to prefer an appeal under section 9(4) of the 1961 Ordinance similar to that as stated in the 4 MLR case or as referred to in section 9 of the Ordinance and, as such, in our opinion the circumstances as stated in the 4 MLR case will not be applicable in the instant case. 

 27. Dr Shirin next referred to the case of Azharuddin Ahmed vs Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.) Dhaka reported in 19 DLR 489 wherein it was held that "Writ jurisdiction can be invoked when an alternative remedy available is not adequate, specific and equally speedy and convenient" and submitted that if the petitioner preferred an application by way of appeal against the impugned order then his office will be taken over by the caretaker body and the said caretaker body would not be competent in conducting religious practices of the Buddhist community. This would seriously undermine the functions of the organisation and create serious obstruction in the administration of the organisation as well as welfare of its members and, as such, it is not a speedy and efficacious remedy. She further submitted that the appeal would have to be heard by a Board to be constituted for the purpose under section 9(3) of the 1961 Ordinance which has not yet been formed and the hearing of the appeal being a time consuming matter it cannot be an equally efficacious remedy. 

 28. We have given our anxious consideration to the submissions of the learned Advocates for the petitioner and the learned Additional Attorney-General. The learned Additional Attorney-General says that the organisation has been set up for the welfare of the Buddhist community and a huge of fund is being remitted to it both from home and abroad and if these funds are not properly administered by the organisation then the community itself will be cheated. The enquiry committee had found that the audited accounts have not been kept properly and some money received as donation from different organisations have not been included in the books of account of petitioner's organisation and, in such circumstances, the regulating authority has not only power to intervene as custodian but also has a duty to protect the interest of the community for which the organisation itself has been set up. No doubt, certain inconveniences may result. These have to be tolerated for the greater interest. The caretaker body is only a temporary measure to hold election from among the members of the community and they are required to act within the provisions of law and thereafter, to hand over the administration of the organisation to the elected representatives. The petitioner could have resorted to the procedure of appeal under section 9(4) of the 1961 Ordinance instead of rushing to this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution. In our opinion, the petitioner has not been able to make out a sufficiently strong case for bypassing the appeal provided by the Ordinance itself and in that view of the matter also the instant Writ petition is not maintainable. In our opinion the Registration Authority on perusal of the enquiry report had sufficient grounds to be satisfied that intervention was necessary and, as such, has acted within its powers to pass the impugned order of suspending the Executive Committee of Bangladesh Bouddha Kristi Prachar Sangha under section 9(1) of the Voluntary Social Welfare Agencies (Registration and Control) Ordinance, 1961 in order to establish proper administration by removing irregularities as per direction of the Ministry of Social Welfare (vide letter bearing Memo No. Sha Mau/ Proti/ Sha/ NGO12/ 2001 668 dated 26-11-2001 as contained in Annexure B.
